Overview

A poor diet does not just affect your weight — it can cause serious, long-term health conditions that affect the heart, bones, teeth, blood and the body's ability to manage blood sugar. This lesson focuses on six diet-related health risks: obesity, coronary heart disease (CHD), bone diseases (rickets and osteoporosis), dental decay, iron deficiency anaemia and type 2 diabetes.

You need to understand the cause of each condition, the dietary factors that contribute to it, and the groups most at risk. Examiners expect you to link specific nutrients to specific conditions with precision.

Obesity

Obesity occurs when a person's BMI reaches 30 or above. It is caused by a sustained energy imbalance — when energy intake from food consistently exceeds the energy the body uses through basal metabolic rate and physical activity. The excess energy is stored as body fat.

Obesity significantly increases the risk of several serious conditions:

  • Type 2 diabetes — excess body fat makes cells resistant to insulin
  • Coronary heart disease (CHD) — obesity raises blood cholesterol and blood pressure
  • Certain cancers — including bowel, breast and kidney cancer
  • Joint problems — excess weight puts strain on weight-bearing joints such as knees and hips, increasing the risk of osteoarthritis
Key Fact

Obesity is defined as a BMI of 30 or above. It is caused by energy in exceeding energy out over a sustained period. It increases the risk of type 2 diabetes, CHD, certain cancers and joint problems. Prevention focuses on balancing energy intake with physical activity.

Coronary Heart Disease (CHD)

Coronary heart disease occurs when fatty deposits build up inside the coronary arteries — the blood vessels that supply the heart muscle with oxygen. Over time, these deposits narrow the arteries, restricting blood flow. If an artery becomes completely blocked, it causes a heart attack.

Two dietary factors are particularly important:

A diet high in saturated fat raises blood cholesterol levels. When there is too much cholesterol in the blood, it is deposited on the walls of arteries, forming fatty plaques. These plaques narrow the arteries and reduce blood flow to the heart. Saturated fat is found in butter, cheese, fatty cuts of meat, cakes, biscuits and palm oil.

To reduce the risk: replace saturated fats with unsaturated fats (such as olive oil and rapeseed oil), eat oily fish twice a week, and increase intake of soluble fibre from oats, beans and lentils — which helps to lower cholesterol.

A diet high in salt causes the body to retain water, which increases blood volume and raises blood pressure. High blood pressure (hypertension) damages the walls of arteries and makes it easier for fatty deposits to accumulate. Adults should consume no more than 6g of salt per day.

To reduce salt intake: use herbs and spices for flavour instead of salt, avoid processed foods (which contain hidden salt), and check food labels for sodium content. Around 75% of the salt people eat comes from processed foods rather than salt added at the table.

Key Fact — CHD Pathway

High saturated fat → raised blood cholesterol → fatty deposits in artery walls → narrowed arteries → reduced blood flow → heart attack. High salt → water retention → raised blood pressure → damaged artery walls → increased risk of CHD and stroke.

Bone Diseases: Rickets and Osteoporosis

Two important bone conditions are linked to dietary deficiencies:

Rickets is a childhood condition caused by a lack of vitamin D and/or calcium. Without enough of these nutrients, bones cannot mineralise properly and remain soft and weak. This can cause bowed legs, bone pain and poor growth.

Vitamin D is needed to absorb calcium from food. The body makes vitamin D when skin is exposed to sunlight, but dietary sources are also important — especially oily fish, eggs, fortified cereals and fortified margarine. Children who spend little time outdoors, or who have darker skin (which produces less vitamin D from sunlight), are at greater risk.

Osteoporosis is a condition that mainly affects elderly people, particularly post-menopausal women. Bones gradually lose density and become fragile and brittle, making fractures much more likely — especially in the hip, wrist and spine.

A lifetime of insufficient calcium and vitamin D intake contributes to osteoporosis. Calcium-rich foods include milk, cheese, yoghurt, canned fish with bones (sardines), and green leafy vegetables (broccoli, kale). Weight-bearing exercise also helps maintain bone density.

Dental Decay

Dental decay (also called dental caries or tooth decay) occurs when bacteria in the mouth feed on sugars from food and drink. As the bacteria break down the sugars, they produce acid. This acid attacks the hard outer layer of the tooth — the enamel — gradually dissolving it. Over time, this creates holes (cavities) in the teeth.

The more frequently sugary foods and drinks are consumed, the more often the teeth are under acid attack. Sticky, sugary foods are particularly harmful because they cling to the teeth for longer. The risk increases with the frequency of sugar intake, not just the total amount.

Key Fact

The pathway of dental decay: sugars in food → bacteria feed on sugars → acid produced → enamel dissolves → cavities form. It is the frequency of sugar consumption that matters most, not just the quantity. Limiting sugary snacks between meals reduces the number of acid attacks on teeth.

Iron Deficiency Anaemia

Iron deficiency anaemia occurs when the body does not have enough iron to produce adequate amounts of haemoglobin — the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen around the body. Without enough haemoglobin, cells do not receive sufficient oxygen, leading to tiredness, pale skin, breathlessness and difficulty concentrating.

Teenage girls are at particular risk because they lose iron through menstruation. If their diet does not replace this lost iron, anaemia can develop. Girls aged 11–18 need 14.8mg of iron per day.

Vegetarians and vegans are also at increased risk because the most easily absorbed form of iron (haem iron) comes from animal sources such as red meat, liver and kidney. Plant-based iron (non-haem iron) from spinach, lentils, beans and fortified cereals is less readily absorbed by the body.

Vitamin C aids iron absorption. Eating vitamin C-rich foods (such as oranges, peppers or tomatoes) at the same meal as iron-rich foods significantly increases the amount of non-haem iron the body absorbs. This is especially important for vegetarians and vegans.

Key Fact — Iron Absorption

There are two forms of dietary iron: haem iron (from animal sources — easily absorbed) and non-haem iron (from plant sources — less easily absorbed). Consuming vitamin C alongside non-haem iron significantly improves absorption. Tea and coffee can reduce iron absorption.

Type 2 Diabetes

Type 2 diabetes is a condition where the body's cells stop responding properly to insulin — the hormone that controls blood sugar levels. This is called insulin resistance. As a result, glucose remains in the blood instead of entering cells for energy, causing blood sugar levels to rise dangerously.

Type 2 diabetes is strongly linked to:

  • Obesity — excess body fat, particularly around the abdomen, increases insulin resistance
  • A diet high in sugar and refined carbohydrates — causes repeated blood sugar spikes that strain the body's insulin response over time
  • Physical inactivity — exercise helps cells use glucose more effectively

Type 2 diabetes can be managed and sometimes reversed through dietary changes, weight loss and regular exercise. Key dietary strategies include reducing sugar and refined carbohydrate intake, eating more wholegrain foods (which release energy slowly), increasing fibre intake, and maintaining a healthy weight through energy balance.

Key Fact

Type 2 diabetes is caused by insulin resistance — the body's cells stop responding to insulin, so blood sugar stays high. It is strongly linked to obesity, high sugar diets and inactivity. Management includes diet modification, weight loss and exercise.
